scenes.title: Receive the rush without going flat-footed
scenes.objective: Read a defender’s space and support against an approaching carrier.
scenes.briefing: Gold 1 carries toward your Navy net. YOU are the defender between Gold 1 and that net. C is recovering through the middle; no closing speed is specified. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: YOU are closer to Navy’s net than Gold 1 and are the closest shown defender to that net.

questions.prompt: Which player is between the puck carrier and the defending net?
questions.explanation: YOU are closer to Navy’s net than Gold 1 and are the closest shown defender to that net.

questions.prompt: Which two things would you need before deciding how quickly to close?

options.text: A fixed gap that suits every attacker

questions.explanation: Distance alone cannot determine a safe closing action; speed and support are missing or changing.

questions.prompt: Arrange a read before managing this gap.

options.text: Adjust while keeping a useful defensive position

questions.explanation: The routine is conditional; the still image cannot measure the speed needed.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to another example position between Gold 1 and the net.
questions.explanation: The reference preserves net-side position. Whether retreating this far is useful depends on actual speed and support.

questions.prompt: With C back alongside Gold 1, which two checks help you defend together?

options.text: Reassess whether you still need to cover the rush alone
Stop tracking Gold 2 because C has returned
Communicate which threat C can help cover

questions.explanation: Recovering help can change responsibilities, but communication and the second attacker still matter.

questions.prompt: Why is the drawn distance insufficient to prescribe an exact gap?
questions.explanation: Include skating speed, direction, pressure and support; none can be fully proved by one still picture.

questions.prompt: Who is the closest shown defender to Navy’s net?
questions.explanation: YOU are drawn between Gold 1 and the Navy net, so inside protection is first; if C arrives, communicate the next assignment.

questions.prompt: Which two positions should YOU account for before deciding whether recovering help changes your gap?

options.text: C is still farther from Navy’s net than Gold 1
Gold 2 is a separate attacker on the other side of the middle from C
Gold 2 is nearer Navy’s net than Gold 1

questions.explanation: C is still behind Gold 1 relative to the defended left net, while Gold 2 is a separate threat across the middle. That does not tell YOU whether C can arrive in time. Keep both attackers in the read and communicate before changing responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare another net-side position against Gold 1.
questions.explanation: The example stays closer to Navy’s net than Gold 1 and slightly reduces the gap. It does not establish gaze or recovery speed. If Gold 1 passes, reassess responsibilities with C rather than both automatically chasing the new carrier.

questions.prompt: How does C’s recovery change your job without prescribing a fixed gap?
questions.explanation: C’s position can provide help or require YOU to contain longer, so read the carrier and support together; if C is late, protect the middle.

scenes.title: Angle from the middle toward the wall
scenes.objective: Protect the middle while retaining a route back toward the net.
scenes.briefing: Gold 1 carries in a wide neutral-zone lane toward Navy’s left net. YOU approach from nearer the middle. The drill asks YOU to influence the carrier toward the boards while preserving a recovery route. D1 is closer to Navy’s net; skating speed is not specified.
cues: Gold 1 is in a wide neutral-zone lane.
YOU start nearer the middle; D1 is closer to Navy’s net.

questions.prompt: Where is Gold 1 carrying the puck?
questions.explanation: Gold 1 is between the blue lines and nearer the side boards than the middle.

questions.prompt: Which two relationships fit the stated angling goal?

options.text: An approach that gives Gold 1 the middle for free
A route that permits recovery toward the Navy net

questions.explanation: The objective is to influence space while preserving recovery, not simply to arrive first.

questions.prompt: Order one angling read from this freeze.

options.text: Notice Gold 1’s route and your net
Update when Gold 1 passes or changes direction

questions.explanation: The approach changes with the carrier; this is not a fixed collision route.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare an inside, net-side approach to Gold 1.
questions.explanation: This reference stays inside Gold 1 and closer to the defending net. Several approach angles may satisfy the same relationship.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 receives and controls a pass at the shown position, which Navy defender starts closer to that new carrier?
questions.explanation: D1 starts closer to Gold 2 than YOU do. Use that information when communicating about the new threat and your recovery. It does not establish who can close in time or require both defenders to follow the new puck carrier.

questions.prompt: Why can a fast approach be unhelpful if it sends you past Gold 1?
questions.explanation: Explain how overshooting may leave the middle or recovery route available to the attacker.

questions.prompt: Which teammate can support behind YOU if Gold 1 turns inside?
questions.explanation: D1 is positioned deeper behind YOU and can support recovery if Gold 1 turns inside; if D1 is pulled away, protect the route back to Navy’s net yourself.

questions.prompt: Which two conditions support an inside angle?

options.text: YOU can work toward a net-side approach

questions.explanation: Inside position protects the net and D1 provides recovery support; skating past loses both control and angle.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward Navy’s net while staying nearer the middle than Gold 1.
questions.explanation: The example stays inside Gold 1 but is level along the rink’s length, not clearly net-side. It is a comparison point, not proof the carrier stays outside. Recheck speed, recovery and D1’s coverage.

questions.prompt: Why is the wall the preferred direction in this angle, while still requiring a read?
questions.explanation: The drill aims to limit middle access, but speed, passing and support change the next decision. Gold 2 is already inside, so coordinate that threat with D1.

scenes.title: See the far-side player in the low slot
scenes.objective: Balance puck awareness with an off-puck threat near the net.
scenes.briefing: Gold 1 controls the puck at the puck-side half wall. Gold 2 waits across the low slot. YOU are the weak-side defender and the coach has assigned you to stay aware of Gold 2 while D1 pressures the puck. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The briefing names Gold 2 as your off-puck responsibility.

questions.prompt: Which opponent is the assigned off-puck threat?
questions.explanation: The briefing names Gold 2 as your off-puck responsibility.

questions.prompt: Select two things to keep in view.

options.text: Only the puck until a pass is made

questions.explanation: Seeing both may require repeated head checks; watching one permanently is not enough.

questions.prompt: Arrange one weak-side checking routine.

options.text: Check the puck and possible pass

questions.explanation: Checks repeat as the situation moves. The routine does not prescribe a single coverage system.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a net-side position near the low slot.
questions.explanation: The example is closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2. Keep checking the puck and opponent; position alone does not establish what YOU can see.

questions.prompt: Which relationship needs attention before YOU treat the low-slot threat as covered?

options.text: Gold 2 is closer to Navy’s net than YOU are
YOU are closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2 is

questions.explanation: Gold 2 is currently nearer the defended net than YOU. That is a coverage concern to account for while checking the puck and communicating with D1. A future adjustment should respond to the actual threat; this still frame does not prove a pass, shot or required tracking route.

questions.prompt: Describe a way to check the half wall without forgetting the low-slot threat.
questions.explanation: Mention repeated scans, body orientation or communication with D1; avoid claiming you can see everything continuously.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call while D1 pressures Gold 1 on the wall?

options.text: Gold 2 is in the low slot

questions.explanation: Calling Gold 2’s low-slot location keeps the off-puck threat in the switch conversation while D1 pressures; if Gold 2 moves higher, update the coverage lane.

questions.prompt: Which two checks let YOU support without puck-chasing?

options.text: Whether YOU should follow D1’s pressure and leave Gold 2 to the goalie

questions.explanation: The off-puck threat and D1’s pressure define your coverage lane; staring only at puck can lose Gold 2.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a net-side position near Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The example is closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2. Recheck the puck and threat, and communicate any coverage change rather than following a fixed spot.

questions.prompt: How can you check the puck side without abandoning Gold 2?
questions.explanation: Seek a position between Gold 2 and Navy’s net while repeatedly checking the puck and communicating with D1. Do not leave Gold 2 between YOU and the net as a default coverage rule; adjust to the actual threat and team plan.

scenes.title: Recover through useful middle ice
scenes.objective: Choose a recovery relationship to an inside attacking threat.
scenes.briefing: Gold 1 carries toward the Navy net near the side boards. Gold 2 is the inside support player. YOU are recovering behind the rush; D1 is already between Gold 1 and the net. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: Gold 2 is in the middle of the ice while Gold 1 is wide near the side boards.
Gold 1 carries toward the Navy net near the side boards. Gold 2 is the inside support player. YOU are recovering behind the rush; D1 is already between Gold 1 and the net.

questions.prompt: Which attacker is the inside support option?
questions.explanation: Gold 2 is in the middle of the ice while Gold 1 is wide near the side boards.

questions.prompt: Which two starting relationships matter when YOU plan to help the recovery?

options.text: YOU are farther from Navy’s end along the rink than both gold attackers
D1 is closer to Gold 1 than YOU are
YOU are already between both gold attackers and Navy’s net

questions.explanation: YOU are still behind both attackers along the rink, and D1 is nearer Gold 1. Those facts matter when coordinating recovery toward the separate inside threat. They do not prove D1 has stopped the carrier or that YOU can reach a particular target in time.

questions.prompt: Arrange one recovery decision.

options.text: Recover toward a useful net-side relationship

questions.explanation: The reference routine does not prove YOU can win a race from this still picture.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to illustrate recovery through the middle toward Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The example moves toward inside danger rather than duplicating D1’s wide pressure. Whether it is reachable needs timing evidence.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 receives the pass before you arrive, what changes?

options.text: Gold 1 remains the puck carrier automatically
Your route no longer depends on the puck
Gold 2 becomes the puck threat to read

questions.explanation: The recovery job updates with possession; communicate with D1 about the new carrier.

questions.prompt: How would you know you are helping D1 rather than duplicating D1’s job?
questions.explanation: Describe coverage of another threat or lane while retaining awareness of the carrier.

questions.prompt: Which Navy defender starts closer to the net than Gold 1?
questions.explanation: D1 starts net-side of Gold 1. YOU are still recovering; communicate which threat each defender can cover rather than assuming coverage is complete.

questions.prompt: Which two facts shape your useful recovery?

options.text: D1 already sits between Gold 1 and the net
Whether Gold 1 is the only threat because D1 has the carrier

questions.explanation: D1’s coverage and Gold 2’s inside route divide the jobs; a puck-only chase duplicates D1.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example middle recovery target closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The target is net-side of Gold 2 and in the middle. The image cannot prove YOU can reach it in time. If possession changes, reassess responsibilities with D1.

questions.prompt: How would you know you are helping D1 rather than skating into D1’s job?
questions.explanation: Cover the inside support while D1 faces the wide carrier, then communicate the handoff; if D1 loses the route, switch to the nearest danger.

scenes.title: Decide before leaving the net front
scenes.objective: Avoid duplicating a teammate’s pressure without checking coverage.
scenes.briefing: D1 pressures Gold 1 in the puck-side corner. YOU are near the net front. Gold 2 is in the slot. The coach’s stated plan has D1 contesting the corner while YOU protect the inside threat. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: Gold 2 is central in the defending zone, nearer the slot than either wall.

questions.prompt: Where is the off-puck attacker Gold 2?

options.text: At the attacking blue line on the right

questions.explanation: Gold 2 is central in the defending zone, nearer the slot than either wall.

questions.prompt: Which two defender-to-attacker relationships support the stated division of jobs in this view?

options.text: D1 is nearer Gold 1 than YOU are
YOU are nearer Gold 2 than D1 is
Gold 2 is farther toward the side boards than either Navy defender

questions.explanation: D1 is nearer the corner carrier and YOU are nearer the inside attacker. Those positions fit the stated plan, but do not prove containment or forbid helping. If the puck threat changes, communicate who can account for each attacker before changing jobs.

questions.prompt: Arrange a read before leaving the net front.
questions.explanation: This follows the exercise’s coverage plan, not a universal requirement for every defensive system.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare another inside position between Gold 2 and the net.
questions.explanation: This keeps a net-side relationship while retaining a possible view of the corner. Other coverage shapes may differ.

questions.prompt: D1 falls and Gold 1 gains a path toward the net. What changes?

options.text: Treat the old corner assignment as unchangeable
Leave Gold 1’s new path out of the read
Reassess the immediate puck threat and coordinate coverage

questions.explanation: A new immediate threat can require an adjustment; the scenario does not dictate a universal switch.

questions.prompt: How could both defenders chasing the corner make Gold 1’s job easier?
questions.explanation: Gold 1 may gain a pass to Gold 2 or open inside ice. Explain the tradeoff rather than saying support is always wrong.

questions.prompt: Which Navy teammate’s corner pressure should YOU confirm before leaving the net front?
questions.explanation: D1 is assigned to contest the corner. Before changing position, check the immediate puck danger and who can cover Gold 2. If D1 falls, reassess both threats and communicate.

questions.prompt: Which two checks precede leaving the net front?
questions.explanation: D1’s pressure and Gold 2’s net-side route tell YOU whether leaving helps; corner activity alone does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to the lane between Gold 2 and the Navy net.
questions.explanation: The example lies in the lane between Gold 2 and Navy’s net. If Gold 1 wins inside, reassess the immediate threat and coordinate coverage rather than automatically abandoning Gold 2.

questions.prompt: If YOU decide to leave the net front, what should YOU communicate to D1 before making the move?
questions.explanation: A short call — such as confirming D1 has Gold 1 contained, or telling D1 that YOU are stepping away from the net front — helps D1 adjust instead of being surprised. There is no single required wording, and what YOU say can change with what D1 signals back.
